u1l1: Count the legs: in the playground, look for an insect and a spider and, without touching them, count their legs from a distance. On the board, draw both: six legs versus eight.
u1l2: Modeling-clay insect: each child makes an insect from three balls (head, thorax and abdomen) and adds the legs to the thorax with toothpicks or paper strips.
u1l3: Made-up insect: draw a new insect with six legs and two pairs of wings. A classmate checks that everything comes out of the thorax.
u1l4: Detective antennae: with your eyes closed, smell three jars (cinnamon, lemon and coffee) and guess what they are. That's how insects find food: they pick up smells with their antennae.
u1l5: Eat like an insect: drink juice with a straw (sucking) and break a cookie with a clothespin (chewing). Which mouth is each tool like?
u2l1: Hiding-place map: walk around the playground or garden and mark on a plan where there are more plants, damp or shade. Where do you think more insects live? Check by looking, without suddenly lifting stones.
u2l2: Secret signals: in pairs, invent a signal with a flashlight or with claps to find each other in class, like fireflies do with their light and crickets with their song.
u2l3: Life-cycle cards: draw egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and butterfly on four cards, shuffle them and put them in order as a group.
u2l4: Two cycles: on the board, put the butterfly's life cycle (four stages) next to the grasshopper's (three). Which stage is the grasshopper missing?
u3l1: Scaly wings: use a magnifying glass on an enlarged photo of a butterfly wing (or a wing you find on the ground, never from a live butterfly) and draw the mosaic of scales.
u3l2: The pencil case: open and close a pencil case to see how the elytra keep and protect the thin wings the beetle flies with.
u3l3: Beehive class: share out a short task like in a beehive (scouts, carers and guards). Afterwards, talk about why teamwork works so well for them.
u3l4: Water detectives: if there's a river or pond nearby, go and look for dragonflies (from the bank and with an adult). Lots of them is usually a clue that the water is clean.
u3l5: Super jumps: measure how far each child jumps and how many times their height it is. A grasshopper jumps about twenty times its length. How far would you jump?
u3l6: Sipping sap: with a thin straw, sip colored water from a sponge, the way true bugs suck plant juice (sap) with their needle mouths.
u3l7: Recyclers: leave a piece of fruit in a jar covered with thin cloth and look at it every day without opening it. Mold will grow: fungi that break the fruit down. Talk about who cleans up nature: fungi, beetles, and many flies and their larvae do that job.
u4l1: Breakfast without insects: write down what you have for breakfast and cross out what wouldn't exist without pollinating insects (fruit, chocolate, coffee…). What's left?
u4l2: Ladybugs to the rescue: in the playground, play tag: some are aphids and others are ladybugs that catch them. That's how a pest is controlled without poison.
u4l3: Still-water patrol: make a list of places at school or at home where water collects (buckets, tires, vases) and how to empty them so mosquitoes can't breed.
u4l4: Forest ranger mural: split a mural into three parts (Harmless, Can be a pest and Careful) and have each group stick their drawings in the right place, explaining why.
u5l1: Living map: on a big sheet of paper, draw a map of Venezuela with the plains, the Andes, the rainforest, the coast and the islands. Each group picks a landscape, tells what it's like (cold or hot? lots of rain or little?) and draws an insect that lives there.
u5l2: Cocuyo or firefly?: turn off the classroom lights. One child is the cocuyo, with two flashlights covered in green paper that stay on, and another is the firefly, turning a single one on and off. Who can guess which is which?
u5l3: Blue without paint: blow soap bubbles and look at them in the light. The colors change as they move, even though nobody painted them: something similar happens with the morpho's blue. Then everyone draws their own 88 butterfly.
u5l4: Leafcutter line: in the playground, form a line; each child carries a little piece of green paper from one side to the other and leaves it in the “nest.” At the end, talk about it: what do real leafcutter ants do with the leaves?
u5l5: Where's the stick insect?: hide brown and green paper sticks around the classroom or the playground. Which ones are harder to find? That's how disguise works. At the end, pick up every piece of paper.
u5l6: Ranger poster: together, make a poster with three things the class will do to take care of Venezuela's insects, and hang it in the classroom.
u6l1: Arthropod family: draw a chart on the board with columns for 6, 8, 14 and lots and lots of legs, and have each group draw an animal in its column. Then bend your elbows, knees and fingers: we have joints too, but our skeleton is on the inside!
u6l2: Yarn spider web: sit in a circle and pass a ball of yarn around, holding on to your end, until you've spun a web. Drop a little paper ball on it: that's the fly. Who can feel the thread shake, like a spider does with its legs?
u6l3: Glass-and-card rescue: with a paper or toy spider, practice in pairs how to cover it with a glass, slide a piece of card underneath and let it go outside. Remember: with real spiders, an adult always does it.
u6l4: Myriapod race: make two lines holding each other's shoulders. In the centipede, one child behind another (one pair of feet per ring), and it moves fast. In the millipede, two by two, side by side (two pairs per ring); it goes slowly and, when it hears “danger!”, it curls into a spiral.
u6l5: Sun or shade?: with the teacher, find a damp, shady spot in the schoolyard and a dry, sunny one. The teacher slowly lifts a stone or flowerpot in each and everyone looks without touching: where are there more pill bugs? Why might that be? When you're done, put it back the way it was.
u6l6: Leg detectives: each child draws a critter on a card without saying what it is. The others count legs, body parts and antennae to guess whether it's an insect, an arachnid, a myriapod or a crustacean.
u7l1: Chains on the board: each child draws a living thing (a plant, a caterpillar, a grasshopper, a bird, a frog…) and together they join them with arrows or yarn to make chains of who eats whom. They always start with a plant.
u7l2: Cotton-ball bee: make a paper flower with string stamens dipped in cornmeal at the tip (the pollen). Use a cotton ball as the bee: touch the stamens and then the pistil of a classmate's flower. Did the pollen move?
u7l3: Recycling jar: in a clear jar put damp soil, dry leaves and fruit peels, cover it with a piece of cloth and look at it every week. Write down how the leftovers break down and whether fungi appear.
u7l4: Where is it?: hide paper insects around the classroom painted the color of their spot (green on a plant, brown on wood) and others red with black spots. Which ones do you find first? Talk about why.
u7l5: Colony in the playground: hand out the jobs (a queen, workers who find food, workers who care for the young and soldiers who defend the nest) and carry paper balls to the nest together. What happens if nobody does one of the jobs?
u7l6: Yarn web: in a circle, each child is a living thing (bee, flower, bird, fungus…) and passes a ball of yarn to someone they're connected to. Then the “bee” lets go of its thread: who feels the web go slack?
u8l1: Playground scientists: in pairs, choose a corner of the playground and watch it quietly for 5 minutes, with a magnifying glass if you have one. Write down the date, time and place, and draw what you see without touching anything. Then compare your notebooks.
u8l2: Question factory: each group writes three questions about the insects in the playground. Together, decide which ones can be checked by looking or counting, and write a hypothesis for each one.
u8l3: The flower experiment: put two pots of flowers of different colors in the playground. Taking turns, count for 5 minutes the insects that visit each one, at the same time of day, and make a chart on the board. Was your hypothesis right?
u8l4: Class hotel: together, fill an old wooden box with hollow canes, pine cones and tightly packed twigs (an adult cuts the canes). Decide together on the best spot: morning sun, out of the rain and near flowers.
u8l5: Helping map: draw a big map of the school and mark where you could plant flowers, which lights could be turned off at night and where to leave a wild corner. Choose one of those actions and do it together.
u8l6: The promise tree: each child writes or draws their forest ranger promise (observe, respect, care and teach) on a leaf-shaped piece of paper, and together you build a big tree on the classroom wall.
